Title: Safar dar Watan - Spotify Podcast
Subject: Podcast
Description: "سفر در وطن" : A Journey Home, explores the spirit of Kashmir, where each soul is a traveler on a journey home. Title: Parihaspora : The City of Laughter
Subject:
On this episode of Safar Dar Watan, we travel to Parihāsapura, the legendary "City of Laughter," perched above the Vitasta (now the Jhelum River) in the Kashmir Valley. Founded by Lalitaditya Muktapida in the mid-8th century CE, this was more than a capital—it was an epicenter of artistry, devotion, and urban grandeur.

Lalitaditya's vision came alive in four majestic temples adorned with colossal gold, silver, and bronze images—some towering over 4 meters tall. Monasteries, palaces, and royal avenues connected sacred and secular life. Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī immortalizes its brilliance, and explorers like Al-Bīrūnī and Abū’l-Fazl later noted its vast, haunting ruins.

The city declined after the court returned to Srinagar. Its sacred structures were cannibalized by later rulers, and a deliberate diversion of the Vitasta by Soya Pandit under King Avantivarman (855–883 CE) transformed its fertile foothills into wetlands—severing its lifeblood and its legacy.

Today, only stones remain. Yet the stones still speak of power, faith, and an imperial dream that once soared above the valley.

This is Parihaspora… and this is Safar Dar Watan.
Creator: Aania Sayida Mir

Title: Etchings in stone : Voices of Kashmir's Architectural Epigraphy
Subject: Architectural Epigraphy
Description:
How do buildings speak?
Through carved verses, poetic inscriptions, and words etched into their very walls. In this episode, Safar Dar Watan explores the world of architectural epigraphy — the art and history of inscriptions carved on stone, wood, and metal across Kashmir’s built heritage. Through the exhibition Naqsh… The Imprint, curated by Dr. Haakim Sameer Hamdani and his team at the School of Architecture and Planning, Islamic University of Science & Technology (IUST), Awantipora, we uncover how these inscriptions serve as voices from the past — revealing devotion, identity, and cultural exchange.
Supported by a Conservation Grant from the Barakat Trust (U.K.), this year-long (2023–24) project surveyed over 600 sites across Kashmir, studying 41 inscriptions in depth — from mosques and shrines to bridges and mausoleums. Featuring reflections from Dr. Haakim Sameer Hamdani, an architectural historian based in Srinagar, who completed his post-doctoral fellowship at MIT. His previous works include City of Kashmir, Shi‘ism in Kashmir: A History of Sunni–Shia Rivalry and Reconciliation and The Syncretic Traditions of Islamic Religious Architecture of Kashmir.Each stone carries a story — of patrons and artisans, of language and belief, of continuity and change. These inscriptions remind us that history is not only written in books, but engraved in the architecture that surrounds us.This episode is both a tribute and a call — to preserve, to listen, and to remember. </p>

Title: Research paper entitled "What is Worth Preserving in Digital Archiving? Community, Consent and an Exploration of the Psychology of Preservation"
Subject: This  research  critically  examines  the  epistemological,  ethical,  and  methodological  dimensions  of  digital archiving  in  the  preservation  of  Kashmiri  cultural  heritage.  Anchored  in  the  central  question-what  is worth  preserving  in  digital  archiving?-The  study  interrogates  how  intangible  and  vernacular  heritage practices are engaged, contested, or excluded in technologically mediated preservation efforts. Utilizing a qualitative   ethnographic   framework,   the   research   incorporates   seven   semi-structured   interviews conducted through a publicly accessible podcast series on Spotify, each of which explores the psychology of preservation from intergenerational, gendered, and community-based  perspectives. Complemented  by field  documentation  at  historically  and  spiritually  significant  sites  in  Srinagar,  the  study  identifies persistent patterns of resistance to visual documentation, particularly in sacred spaces. These refusals are not seen as obstacles but as expressions of cultural self-respect-showing a desire to control how traditions are represented, protect spiritual spaces, and build trust in how archiving is done.The research evaluates the  affordances  and  limitations  of  digital  tools-including  artificial  intelligence,  virtual  reality,  3D mapping,  and  open-access  community  platforms-through  the  lens  of  critical  heritage  studies  and decolonial methodology. Findings suggest that while these technologies offer preservation potential, their implementation  often  reproduces  extractive  paradigms  unless  grounded  in  participatory  and  values-led approaches. This study contributes to the broader discourse on intangible heritage, postcolonial memory, and  community-based  archiving  by  advocating  for  preservation  as  an  ethical,  dialogic,  and  negotiated process.  It  calls  for  a  reconfiguration  of  digital  archiving  as  a  co-constructed  practice,  one  that  resists authorized  heritage  discourses  and  centers  lived  experience,  affective  knowledge,  and  cultural  self-determination.
